faq: How do I know the summary is correct?
Each summary links back to its source and, in the Premium package, to the page. A person should still check anything important, since summaries can miss nuance or get a detail wrong.
Can it summarize very long documents?
Yes, in sections. Long reports are split, summarized part by part and joined into one overview. We agree a page limit per package before we start so scope is clear.
Can summaries be written in my team's style?
Yes. Send two or three examples of summaries you like and we shape the format, length and wording to match. The style is written down so it stays consistent.
Is it safe for confidential documents?
We work inside your own accounts and only on the documents you choose. If something is sensitive, tell us first and we can use masked samples while we build.

desc:
Document and email thread summaries turn long reports, meeting notes and conversations into a few clear lines. Ecom Swift LLC sets up a summary step in the length and format you choose, with a link back to the source for every point.

## What are document and email thread summaries?

A summary is a short account of a longer item: what it is about, what was decided and what needs action. For a report it may be five lines. For an email thread of forty messages it may be a list of decisions and open questions. The summary always keeps a pointer to the original, so a reader can open the exact page or message behind any statement.

A summary is a way to decide where to spend reading time. It does not replace the source when the details matter.

## Why long documents and threads drain a team

Reports arrive faster than anyone can read them. Email threads grow until a new participant needs half an hour to catch up. Meeting notes are saved and never opened again. People either skim and miss the decision, or read everything and lose the afternoon.

The cost shows up in small ways: a task nobody realized was assigned, a question answered twice, a manager asking for a briefing that someone must write by hand. Reading is necessary work, but not all reading deserves the same depth.

## How summaries speed up decisions

A good summary gets a busy person to the point in under a minute. They see the topic, the decision and the next action, and they can click through only when something needs a closer look. New team members catch up on a thread without interrupting anyone to ask what happened.

Digests make this scale. Instead of dozens of separate documents, a reader gets one daily or weekly page that covers everything new, tagged by topic and name. Accuracy is the key concern, which is why each statement carries a source reference and why we test on your own documents before anything is used for real work.

## What a good summary set-up includes

- A chosen length, such as a few lines for quick scanning or a longer version for detail.
- A fixed layout: topic, key points, decisions and action items.
- Names, dates and amounts kept exactly as they appear in the source.
- A link or page reference for every summary, back to the original.
- Separate formats for different material, such as reports, minutes and email threads.
- Delivery to the place you already read, such as email, chat or a sheet.
- Topic and name tags, so summaries can be searched and filtered.
- Optional digests that bundle new items into one read.
- A short style guide, so the wording fits your team.

## How we work

We begin by reading a handful of your documents and asking what a useful summary would look like for each. We draft the layout, you edit it, and we run the step on real material. A person on your side compares each summary with the source and tells us what is missing or overstated.

We adjust the instructions until summaries consistently carry the right points, and until they stay silent where the source is silent. The Basic package covers one type of document with a short format. Standard handles several types, adds decisions and action items and delivers to email, chat or a sheet in two lengths. Premium creates daily or weekly digests with tags, page references and a style guide for your team.

## Do and avoid

**Do:**
- Read the source whenever a decision carries real risk.
- Keep the source link or page number attached to every summary.
- Tell us which facts must never be altered, such as figures and names.
- Choose a length that matches how people really read.
- Share examples of summaries you find useful.

**Avoid:**
- Acting on a summary of a legal or financial document without opening the original.
- Asking for very short summaries of material full of exceptions.
- Mixing very different document types in one format.
- Forwarding confidential material to tools you have not approved.
- Treating the first test results as final without checking them against the source.

## Who this service is for

It suits a manager who receives long weekly reports and wants the essentials in one message. It suits a project team with busy email threads where decisions get lost. It also suits a founder or consultant with a backlog of meeting notes, who needs a searchable, short record of what was agreed.

## What we need from you

Send a few documents or threads of each type, an example of a summary you would like and a note on who will read them. Tell us how confidential the material is so that we can choose where it is processed. We never need passwords. Access is given by sharing a folder or inviting us as a collaborator or team user, and you control how long it lasts.
